A teddy bear has a rounded head, short protruding muzzle, two small ears high on the head, and a soft torso with four stubby limbs. Its plush fabric may be beige, brown, cream, or another colour, with a visible pile that changes shade when brushed against its grain. The nose is usually stitched or molded; eyes are small dark buttons or securely fixed plastic, depending on the toy. Seams follow the sides of the limbs and body. It slumps when set down, compresses in someone’s arms, and springs back imperfectly. Handling makes a faint fabric rustle, not a mechanical sound.

Inflated latex balloons are smooth, thin-skinned ovals with a narrower neck tied into a small knot. Their colours look saturated in shade and translucent where strong light passes through; a window or ceiling lamp appears as a bright reflection on the curved surface. Air-filled balloons fall slowly, bounce lightly, and roll along the floor. Helium-filled ones pull upward against a narrow curling ribbon, bobbing with drafts or a person’s movement. They squeak when rubbed together and make a light tapping sound against a wall. Party clusters vary slightly in size and shape, even when the colours match.

A wedding cake is commonly presented on a rigid round board or stand, often with two or more round tiers that narrow upward. Smooth buttercream or fondant may cover the sides in white or pale colours, with piped borders, sugar flowers, or fresh flowers placed deliberately along the tiers. The tiers are level but handmade decoration has tiny irregularities; fresh petals cast small shadows. Its height reaches roughly from a person’s waist toward their chest when displayed on a table. A knife meets slight resistance through icing, then softer sponge. Serving produces quiet plate and cutlery clinks amid conversation.

A birthday cake is usually a low round or rectangular sponge cake on a cardboard cake board, covered with buttercream, whipped cream, or glossy icing. Piped edges, coloured sprinkles, fruit, or chocolate pieces sit on top; lettering, if present, follows the cake’s curve and is rarely perfectly uniform. Thin candles stand in the icing, their small flames bending with nearby movement and reflecting on glossy decorations. A person can carry the cake with both hands. Plates and forks clink as it is served, candles make a faint hiss when blown out, and a knife leaves cream on each cut face.

A chocolate box is a shallow, rigid cardboard box, commonly rectangular or square, with a fitted lid. Printed branding belongs on the actual package, not as a floating label; an unbranded box can have a plain coloured lid. Inside, small chocolates sit in individual cavities of a molded plastic tray or pleated paper cups, sometimes beneath a thin protective sheet. Their surfaces range from matte cocoa dust to glossy tempered chocolate, with slight differences in shape and decoration. The lid lifts without hinges and may rub softly against the base. The tray crackles when handled; chocolates make muted taps as they are picked up.

topic: Iraqi tea set on a tray
body: An Iraqi tea service sits on a round metal tray with a shallow raised rim, often stainless steel or engraved brass-coloured metal. Small, clear, handleless istikan glasses have narrow waists and flared lips; each stands on a little saucer. Strong black tea fills the lower part of each glass in a deep reddish amber, leaving room near the rim. A small teapot and sugar bowl may share the tray, with teaspoons resting on saucers. Someone carries the tray level with one hand beneath it or both hands at its edges. Glass and spoon make delicate clinks; poured tea sounds like a thin, steady splash.

A whole watermelon is a heavy oval or round fruit, commonly about the width of a person’s torso, with a smooth, firm rind. Its green skin shows irregular darker green stripes or mottling and a duller patch where it rested on the ground. Cut open, it reveals thick pale rind around red or pink flesh, often dotted with flat dark seeds, though some varieties have only small pale seed traces. The cut surface looks wet and glistens in sunlight. A knife passes through the flesh easily but needs more pressure at the rind. Slices drip juice, thud softly on a plate, and crunch wetly when bitten.

A pomegranate is a round, slightly flattened fruit about the size of a fist, with tough, leathery skin ranging from warm yellow-red to deep crimson. A small, stiff, star-shaped crown protrudes from one end. The skin is matte to faintly glossy and may show natural scuffs or fine cracks. Cutting it reveals pale, spongy membranes separating tightly packed, translucent red or pink arils, each enclosing a seed. A ripe fruit feels heavy. Arils tumble and bounce when loosened into a bowl, making soft taps; biting them gives a crisp pop. In Iraqi markets, whole fruits sit in shallow crates or are split to display their colour.

Oranges are roughly spherical citrus fruits, usually palm-sized, with a dimpled peel coloured bright orange to yellow-orange. Their skins vary in thickness and often show a small green stem scar; some retain a leaf. Beneath the peel is white, fibrous pith around wedge-shaped segments filled with juice sacs. A knife makes a soft rasp through the rind, while peeling releases tiny sprays of aromatic oil. Segments separate with a faint tear and release juice when squeezed. In a fruit stall, oranges pile unevenly in crates rather than forming perfect rows, with natural variation in size, colour and surface marks.

Bananas grow in connected hands, each fruit attached by a short, thick stalk. An individual banana is elongated and gently curved, with several subtle lengthwise ridges and a tapered tip. Market bananas are commonly green-yellow, clear yellow or yellow with scattered brown ripening freckles; the peel may have small pressure bruises. Inside, the flesh is pale cream and soft but holds its shape when freshly peeled. Pulling a peel strip downward makes a faint fibrous rip, and slicing gives a muted tap on a board. Hands of bananas hang from stall hooks or rest in crates, shifting slightly when lifted by their shared stem.

Grapes hang in branching clusters from a thin central stem, with individual berries attached on finer stalks. Berries may be small and round or slightly oval, coloured pale green, amber, red or dark purple depending on the variety. Fresh skins can carry a dusty-looking natural wax bloom, not dirt. A cluster bends under its own weight, and loose berries roll quickly across a table. Pulling one free makes a tiny snap; biting it breaks the taut skin with a soft pop and releases clear juice. At produce stalls, clusters lie in shallow crates, their slender stems visible between the fruit.

Tomatoes and cucumbers are commonly displayed together at Iraqi vegetable stalls and chopped together for salad. Tomatoes are rounded or slightly flattened, with smooth red skin, a small stem scar and moist chambers of seeds inside; some still carry a green, star-shaped calyx. Cucumbers are elongated, firm and dark to medium green, often with faint lengthwise stripes and a subtly bumpy surface. A knife meets tomato skin with slight resistance before releasing juice; cucumber cuts with a sharper, watery crunch. Chopped pieces glisten in a bowl, while whole vegetables roll or shift naturally when picked up from a crate.

Iraqi torshi is a mixture of vegetables preserved in a sharp brine or vinegar liquid, often served beside rice, sandwiches or grilled food. A clear jar or bowl may show cauliflower florets, carrot rounds, cucumber pieces, turnip and peppers packed irregularly together. Colours range from pale cream and orange to green; turnip can appear vivid pink when pickled with beet. The vegetables stay firm enough to crunch rather than collapsing. Liquid clings to each piece and drips back into the jar when lifted with a spoon. Glass clinks softly against the spoon, followed by a wet stir and a crisp bite.

Iraqi amba is a tangy mango pickle or sauce, typically mustard-yellow to deep golden, with a thick, uneven texture rather than the smooth look of bottled juice. Small softened mango pieces may be visible in the spiced liquid. In a jar it coats the glass above the fill line; on a sandwich or plate it spreads in glossy streaks and slowly settles into folds. A spoon lifts it in a heavy ribbon that drops with a soft plop. Amba is commonly added to Iraqi falafel sandwiches and other street food, where its bright colour contrasts with bread, vegetables and browned fried fillings.

Iraqi geymar is a thick, pale ivory dairy cream served at breakfast, often in a shallow dish with dark date syrup poured over or beside it. The cream sits in soft folds or broad scoops, with a delicate wrinkled surface skin and edges that hold their shape. Date syrup is translucent deep brown where thin and nearly black where it pools; it runs slowly into glossy ribbons over the cream. A spoon presses through the dense, yielding geymar with little sound, then lightly taps the dish. Torn samoon or other bread is used to scoop up both, leaving irregular swirls of cream and syrup.

Iraqi lentil soup is a smooth, opaque golden-yellow to orange soup, usually made from red lentils cooked until they lose their shape. It fills a small ceramic bowl nearly to the rim and may have tiny flecks of cumin or black pepper on its surface. It pours in a thick, continuous stream rather than splashing like water. A spoon leaves a shallow trail that slowly closes. Serve it hot with a lemon wedge and flatbread; a squeeze of lemon makes small ripples across the surface. Steam rises in soft wisps under side light. The scene is quiet except for spoon taps against the bowl and bread tearing.

Iraqi biryani is a piled platter of separate long rice grains, predominantly yellow from spices, with some white and deeper orange patches. Chicken pieces or cooked meat sit among small cubes of fried potato, peas, carrots and short browned strands of vermicelli. Raisins and toasted nuts may be scattered over the top; some servings include halved boiled eggs. It is mixed rather than built as perfectly defined layers. A serving spoon lifts loose grains and heavier pieces together, with a few raisins rolling back onto the platter. The rice gives off light steam when fresh. Plates, spoons and small side dishes sit around a family table.

Tepsi baytinjan fills a shallow round or rectangular metal baking tray. Fried eggplant slices show dark purple skin around soft brown centres, overlapping with pale golden potato slices, red tomato rounds and onion. Depending on the household, small meatballs or seasoned minced meat sit between the vegetables. A red tomato sauce pools in the gaps and stains the tray edges; the top has browned spots from the oven, not a thick cheese crust. When a spoon cuts in, tender slices slide apart and sauce runs into the space. The tray may arrive bubbling faintly, then settle with a soft sizzle. Serve beside white rice or bread.

Iraqi fasolia with rice is commonly presented as two distinct parts: a bowl of white beans in red tomato stew beside a mound of steamed white rice. The beans remain whole and plump, with glossy skins; small pieces of lamb or beef may be visible in the sauce. The stew is fluid enough to ladle but thick enough to coat the beans. Iraqi rice has visible separate grains and may have a lightly browned crisp portion from the bottom of the pot. A ladleful of fasolia spreads across the rice and sinks between grains. Gentle steam rises, accompanied by the clink of a ladle and plates.

Makhlama is served hot in a small frying pan or shallow plate, with eggs set among softened chopped tomatoes and onions. The tomatoes make a red, slightly oily sauce with visible skins and irregular pieces, rather than a smooth purée. Egg whites turn opaque while yolks may remain rounded and soft; in other servings, the eggs are stirred into yellow-and-red curds. Some versions contain browned minced meat, but the egg-and-tomato base stays visible. A metal spoon breaks a yolk and draws yellow across the sauce. The pan gives a brief hiss as it leaves the heat. Iraqi bread is used to scoop it up.

A shawarma spit is a tall vertical steel skewer carrying a dense stack of thin meat slices, shaped into a tapered cylinder roughly as high as a worker’s torso. The skewer stands over a circular drip tray, with upright gas burners or electric heating panels behind it. A motor turns the meat slowly and steadily, bringing every side past the heat; the outer layer darkens and glistens while the centre stays covered. A cook shaves thin strips downward with a long knife or electric cutter, and the pieces fall into the tray. There is a low motor hum, burner hiss and crisp scraping sound. Warm shop lights catch the rendered fat.

An Iraqi falafel sandwich often uses a small, elongated samoon loaf with a pointed end and a slit along one side. Several deep-fried falafel pieces sit inside, their rough brown crusts contrasting with a soft greenish interior where one is broken. Chopped tomato, cucumber, parsley and pickles may fill the gaps, with tahini sauce or tangy amba visible near the opening. The bread compresses slightly when held, and loose crumbs or salad pieces can fall onto the paper wrapper. A bite makes a brief crisp crunch followed by the softer sound of bread tearing. It is commonly assembled at a street-food counter.

Scooped ice cream forms rounded mounds with curved ridges left by the scoop. Its surface is matte and faintly grainy when very cold, becoming smoother and glossier as it warms. Vanilla is pale cream, chocolate is brown, and fruit flavours vary in colour; avoid making every flavour unnaturally bright. A scoop sits in a wafer cone or paper cup, visibly smaller than a person’s palm. In warm air, the edges soften first, then slow drips run down the cone or cup. A metal scoop scrapes against the tub, while a wafer cone gives a dry crunch when bitten. Shop display lights reflect on the glass freezer.

A small Iraqi juice shop has a bright Arabic sign above a glass-front counter, with oranges, lemons, pomegranates, and bananas displayed in crates or neat piles. Behind the counter sit a citrus press, blender, plastic pitchers, and rows of clear cups. A worker cuts fruit, presses halves under a metal cone, or runs a blender that buzzes sharply before stopping. Juice pours in a thick, uneven stream; pulp and foam gather at the top. Customers stand close to the counter while cups are filled, lidded, and handed over. Daylight catches condensation on cold pitchers and the wet shine of freshly cut fruit.

A common single-serve Pepsi bottle is clear molded PET plastic, roughly hand-height, with rounded shoulders, a narrow threaded neck, and a five-lobed base that lets it stand upright. Dark brown cola shows through the plastic. A blue wraparound label sits around the middle, carrying the red, white, and blue Pepsi globe and white Pepsi lettering; a blue screw cap seals the neck above a tamper-evident ring. Bottle sizes and label layouts vary by market. When lifted, the thin plastic flexes slightly. Opening the cap makes a short crackle and hiss; pouring produces fizz, rising bubbles, and a brief foam head.

A typical disposable drinking-water bottle is transparent PET plastic, narrow enough to hold in one hand, with a short threaded neck, a screw cap, and a tamper-evident ring left behind when first opened. Its sides often have shallow ribs or molded grip panels; the bottom has raised feet. A paper or plastic label wraps around the center, while the clear water reveals any dents in the bottle wall. The lightweight bottle crinkles when squeezed and springs partly back. Removing the cap makes a small plastic snap. Water glugs from the opening when tilted steeply and leaves clear beads of condensation if chilled.

A takeaway coffee cup is a tall, gently tapered paperboard cylinder, wider at its rolled rim than at its flat base. The inside has a thin liquid-resistant lining. A fitted plastic lid snaps over the rim, usually with a raised drinking spout or small sip opening; some cups have a separate corrugated cardboard sleeve around the middle. Branding, when present, is printed on the outside rather than inside the cup. An adult holds it comfortably in one hand, often by the sleeve. Hot coffee gives off faint steam through the opening. The lid clicks when pressed into place, and the cup makes a soft papery sound when set down.

A cappuccino with latte art sits in a small, wide ceramic cup, often on a matching saucer with a teaspoon beside it. Espresso gives the surface a warm brown edge; finely steamed milk forms a glossy, creamy layer with no large visible bubbles. A white heart or leaf pattern spreads across the brown surface, its curved edges made by the milk pour rather than a printed stencil. The cup is filled close to, but below, the rim. Freshly made, it releases a little steam. The pattern slowly blurs as the cup moves, and the saucer gives a light ceramic clink when lifted or set down.

An Arabic sweets tray is a broad, shallow metal serving tray holding small pastries in orderly rows or clusters. It may mix diamond-cut baklava, rolled pastries, round semolina pieces, and pistachio-topped bites; the exact assortment varies by shop. Golden pastry layers have crisp edges, while syrup gives their surfaces a restrained shine. Chopped green pistachio, pale nuts, and occasional paper cups separate pieces visually. A vendor lifts individual sweets with small tongs onto a plate or into a box. The tongs click against the tray, and flaky pieces make a faint crackle. Display-case lighting reflects off the metal rim and glossy syrup.

Kunafa is commonly presented as a shallow round pastry cooked in a wide metal pan and cut into wedges or squares. One familiar version has a crisp, finely shredded pastry surface, toasted from gold to orange-gold, over a soft white cheese filling. Another uses a finer, compact semolina-like crust. Clear sugar syrup adds a glossy sheen, and crushed green pistachios may be scattered across the top. A server slides a flat spatula beneath a portion; crisp strands shift and crackle while the warm filling can stretch in soft threads as the piece lifts. On a plate, a cut edge shows the thin crust above the thicker filling.

Basbousa is a shallow semolina cake baked in a rectangular or round pan and marked into small squares or diamonds. Its surface is evenly golden brown, slightly grainy rather than smooth, with a whole almond or pistachio sometimes pressed into the center of each portion. Sugar syrup soaks into the cake, leaving a moist sheen without hiding the scored lines. A spatula lifts one piece, exposing a dense, tender crumb made of visible fine grains. It holds its shape but releases a few crumbs at the cut edges. A knife makes a soft scraping sound against the pan, followed by the gentle tap of cake placed on a plate.

The Land Cruiser 300 is a large, tall five-door SUV with a broad, nearly upright grille, rectangular LED headlamps, a high hood and a squared-off rear. Trim changes the grille finish and bumper details, but the Toyota badge sits centrally. Its substantial ground clearance, thick tires and large side mirrors make it noticeably taller than nearby sedans. In Iraqi streets it is often white, silver or black. It rolls with restrained body movement on smooth roads, then rocks gently over bumps; the tires make a low hum. Doors close with a heavy thud, while the engine is muted inside and deeper under acceleration.

The Land Cruiser 70 pickup, commonly called a shas, has a narrow, upright two-door cab, a long exposed cargo bed and a distinctly boxy profile. A flat hood, nearly vertical windshield, prominent mirrors and sturdy bumpers distinguish it from the rounded Land Cruiser 300. The tailgate drops downward on hinges, with Toyota lettering or badging according to model year. Its tall ride height and leaf-sprung rear can make an empty bed bounce sharply over rough pavement. People use the bed for secured supplies or equipment. Expect a firm door slam, noticeable engine and tire noise, and a metallic rattle from loose cargo.

The contemporary Lexus LX is a full-size luxury SUV with a tall cabin, long roof and imposing front end. A broad spindle-shaped grille fills most of the nose, with a Lexus badge at its center, slim LED lamps on either side and an LEXUS wordmark across the tailgate. Large alloy wheels sit beneath squared wheel arches; chrome or dark trim varies by version. It is commonly seen in white, pearl, silver or black near homes and shops. The body settles gently after a speed bump rather than jolting abruptly. Its doors shut with a solid, damped sound, and road noise is subdued inside.

The Nissan Patrol Nismo is a large, high-roof SUV with a performance-styled body kit rather than a low sports-car silhouette. On the familiar Y62 version, a wide grille carries the Nissan badge; sculpted bumpers, deep side skirts, large alloy wheels and thin red accent lines distinguish the Nismo from an ordinary Patrol. A NISMO badge appears at the rear. The cabin remains tall enough for adults to step up into it. White, black and silver examples suit Gulf and Iraqi streets. It moves with the mass of a full-size SUV, leaning slightly in turns. The V8 produces a low rumble that rises clearly under acceleration.

The Kia K5 is a low, wide four-door sedan with a long hood, sweeping roofline and short rear deck. Its narrow front grille joins sharp headlamps; on the 2021–23 design, the daytime running lights form distinctive angular zigzags, while a slim illuminated strip spans the rear. A Kia badge sits on the hood and another on the trunk. The car sits much lower than surrounding SUVs, and passengers bend slightly to enter. In urban traffic its body stays fairly level through turns, with a modest dip when braking. Expect tire hiss on pavement, a light door thunk and restrained engine noise during ordinary driving.

The Kia Sorento is a midsize SUV with a broad hood, upright seating position, five doors and a rear liftgate. Current versions have a wide grille, vertical LED lamp elements, a Kia badge above the grille and another centered on the tailgate; the precise lamp pattern and trim vary by model year. Its roof is lower and body shorter than a full-size Land Cruiser, but it stands clearly above a sedan. Families load bags through the upward-swinging liftgate. On streets it leans mildly through corners and rises once after larger bumps. Doors give a firm thump, with soft tire noise and an audible engine when accelerating.

The 2024-onward Hyundai Santa Fe is a boxy midsize SUV with a nearly flat roof, upright tailgate and broad, squared wheel arches. H-shaped light signatures appear at the front and rear, with HYUNDAI lettering spaced across the tailgate. The rear lamps sit unusually low, below the large rear window. Its tall cabin accommodates passengers and luggage; the tailgate lifts overhead to reveal a wide opening. Parked beside a sedan, it looks much taller but not as long as a full-size Patrol. It turns with a slight body lean and settles softly over road joints. Expect a solid door close, muted tire hiss and gentle engine sound.

The Hyundai Accent is a compact four-door sedan, noticeably narrower and lower than a Santa Fe. Its short hood slopes toward a front grille bearing the Hyundai oval, with headlamps at the outer corners; a small trunk projects behind the rear window. Grille, lamp and taillight shapes differ substantially by year, so match them to one generation rather than mixing designs. White, silver and gray examples are common in everyday street scenes. A driver sits relatively low, and the trunk lid lifts separately from the passenger cabin. The light body reacts quickly to bumps; doors close with a modest click-thud, while tire and engine sounds become more apparent during acceleration.

A full-size pickup with a broad, nearly upright front, a large grille carrying Chevrolet’s bowtie emblem, rectangular headlamp assemblies, and a separate open cargo bed behind the cab. Contemporary versions usually have four doors, a high beltline, large side mirrors, and a tailgate stamped with CHEVROLET or fitted with a centered bowtie, depending on trim. Its bed floor and tailgate look practical and hard-wearing, not upholstered. It sits high beside a person; the bed rail reaches roughly waist to chest height. On the road its suspension gently bobs over bumps, tires hiss on asphalt, and the engine sounds low and throaty when accelerating.

A full-size pickup with a tall, squared hood, broad front grille, C-shaped lighting elements on many recent versions, and a blue oval Ford badge centered in the grille. F-150 badges sit on the front fenders; a separate cargo bed ends in a broad tailgate, often stamped F-150. Common four-door cabs have a short gap between cab and bed. Its aluminum body panels sit over a sturdy frame, with dark wheel-well liners and visible tire sidewalls. It stands tall beside people and leans slightly through turns. Doors shut with a solid clunk; road noise, tire hum, and the engine’s pitch rise as it pulls away.

A large, upright luxury SUV with a long flat roof, tall side windows, a broad shield-shaped grille, and Cadillac’s crest centered at the front. Slim vertical lighting accents frame the front corners; tall red taillamps run up both sides of the rear window. Recent models have large wheels, substantial running boards, and a wide rear liftgate rather than a pickup bed. Its dark glass and polished trim catch sharp highlights under streetlights. It towers over nearby sedans, yet moves smoothly, with mild body lean in corners. Electric motors whir when seats or the liftgate move; inside, road and engine sounds are muted.

A Mercedes-Maybach S-Class is a long luxury sedan, not an SUV. It has a broad grille of closely spaced vertical chrome bars, an upright Mercedes star on the hood, and small Maybach double-M emblems on the rear pillars. Long rear doors and a small fixed window behind each door emphasize the rear passenger space. Some cars wear two-tone paint, with a clean horizontal boundary between colors; others are one color. Chrome outlines the windows and brightens the lower body. It glides with little visible bounce, its doors closing with a dense, soft thud. Engine and tire sounds remain faint inside the quiet cabin.

A long, formal BMW sedan with a tall twin-kidney grille, BMW roundel on the hood, and a broad rear cabin. The current design places narrow daytime running lights above lower, darker headlamp units, giving the front a split-light appearance. Its roof flows into a short trunk, not a rear hatch, and its doors are long and thickly framed. Chrome or dark trim varies by specification; the roundel and kidney grille remain clear identifiers. Large wheels turn slowly at parking speed while the body stays level over smooth roads. Doors close with a firm thump; inside, the engine, tires, and air-conditioning are subdued.

A tall Bentley luxury SUV with a large upright mesh grille, winged Bentley badge above it, and round-looking main headlamps set into a sculpted front. The hood is long for an SUV, while the roof continues over four side doors to a sloping rear liftgate. At the back, slim oval lamps sit on either side of the tailgate. Polished metal surrounds the windows and grille; paint reflects light in broad, smooth bands. It sits high beside a person but moves without the abrupt rocking of a utility truck. The doors close heavily, tires make a soft rushing sound, and acceleration brings a restrained engine growl.

A very large, boxy luxury SUV with a tall polished Pantheon grille, rectangular headlamps, and the small Spirit of Ecstasy figure above the grille when displayed. Its roof is high and nearly level, with an upright windshield and broad, flat-sided doors. The rear passenger doors hinge at the back, so they open opposite the front doors. RR monograms appear on the wheels and body badges. Beside a person, the hood and grille feel unusually tall; the wheels are large but proportionate. It rolls over uneven pavement with little visible shake. Doors shut with a deep muffled thud, while tire and engine noise remain distant inside.

A low, wide performance SUV with four side doors, a steeply sloped windshield, and a roof that tapers toward a rear liftgate. Its sharply creased hood meets angular front air openings and narrow headlamps; the gold Lamborghini bull badge sits on the nose. Large wheels fill the arches, with wide tires and prominent brake hardware visible behind the spokes. The rear has slim angular lamps, broad shoulders, and low exhaust outlets. It sits higher than a sports car but lower-looking than a conventional family SUV. The body stays relatively flat in quick turns; tires rumble, and the engine gives a distinct, rising growl under acceleration.

The Ferrari SF90 Stradale is a very low, wide two-seat coupe with a sharply pointed nose, slim headlights and large black air openings cut into its sculpted bodywork. A small yellow Ferrari shield sits on each front fender; the prancing-horse badge is centered on the nose and rear. Behind the cabin, a glass engine cover reveals mechanical parts. The rear has compact angular lamps and two round exhaust outlets mounted unusually high. Its broad tires fill the wheel arches. At walking speed it can glide almost silently on electric power; under acceleration the engine rises to a sharp, layered roar. Sunlight traces hard highlights across its curves.

A modern Porsche 911 is a low sports coupe with two round headlights set high in its front fenders, a sloping roof and broad rear haunches. The nose carries a small Porsche crest; PORSCHE lettering spans the rear above the model name. A narrow red light strip crosses the back, with an engine grille below the rear window. The cabin has two full-size front seats and two much smaller rear seats. Its doors are long relative to its height, and its tires look especially wide from behind. It rolls smoothly over pavement, then squats slightly under acceleration as a deep, mechanical engine note grows louder.

A modern McLaren road car is a low, two-seat, mid-engine sports coupe with a short nose, a teardrop-shaped glass cabin and deep air channels carved into its sides. Its headlights sit in dark, sculpted recesses; a small McLaren wordmark or speedmark appears on the nose and rear. The exact lamps and vents vary by model, but the doors typically hinge upward and outward, exposing a wide sill that occupants step over. Large wheels sit close to the body corners, and engine vents open behind the doors. It moves with little body lean; acceleration brings a rising engine sound, intake rush and tire noise. Glossy paint reflects streetlights in long, curved streaks.

The Bugatti Chiron is an exceptionally wide, low two-seat coupe with a rounded nose and a black horseshoe-shaped front grille bearing a red Bugatti oval. Each side has a huge C-shaped curve framing the door and side air intake. Four small LED squares form each headlight cluster; one thin red light bar stretches across the rear above the central BUGATTI lettering. A broad rear diffuser and four exhaust openings sit low beneath it. The cabin looks compact beside the massive rear bodywork. On smooth pavement it rides firmly, with a subdued engine rumble at low speed that swells into a dense roar and rushing-air sound under acceleration.

The Nissan GT-R R35 is a broad, angular two-door coupe with a long hood, a relatively upright cabin and muscular rear fenders. A Nissan badge sits above the dark front grille, while a small red-and-silver GT-R emblem appears on the grille and trunk. The rear has four round red lamps, two on each side, and four circular exhaust tips beneath the bumper. A modest raised spoiler crosses the trunk. It is large for a sports coupe, with usable front seats and cramped rear seats. At low speed its drivetrain can make faint mechanical clicks; accelerating produces a deep exhaust growl and a brief hiss as the turbochargers build pressure.

The modern Toyota GR Supra is a compact two-seat coupe with a long rounded hood, a short cabin set toward the rear and swollen rear wheel arches. Its roof has two shallow humps, one above each seat. Slim swept-back headlights and large dark openings shape the front; narrow taillights wrap around the rear corners. Toyota badges sit on the nose and tail, with SUPRA lettering across the back. Some vents are decorative trim rather than open holes. The car sits low beside an adult, with a small rear window and a short trunk lid. It turns with little body lean; acceleration brings a low growl that climbs over the sound of its tires.

A familiar older Mitsubishi Lancer on Iraqi streets is a compact four-door sedan, not the wide-bodied Evolution. Common 1990s-to-early-2000s examples have a modest, slightly boxy profile, narrow grille, simple rectangular or softly rounded lamps, thin door pillars and a separate trunk. The three-diamond Mitsubishi emblem sits at the center of the grille; LANCER lettering is on the trunk. Paint may be white, silver or beige, sometimes faded by sun, with plain wheel covers and dusty lower panels. It carries four or five people at ordinary road speed, its suspension bobbing over uneven pavement. Door latches click sharply, and the small engine makes a steady, unpolished hum.

A typical modern Volkswagen Golf is a compact hatchback with a short hood, upright rear window and rear door that lifts together with the glass. The round VW emblem sits in the center of the narrow front grille and again on the hatch, usually above GOLF lettering. It has five doors, a fairly flat roof and room for adults in both rows; the body is much taller and shorter than a sports coupe. Standard versions have restrained bumpers and no oversized wing. The hatch swings upward on gas struts, and the doors close with a solid thud. On the road it moves with modest body lean and a quiet engine-and-tire hum.

On an Iraqi street, the old Brazilian-built Volkswagen Passat is a compact, low car with a long, straight bonnet, thin roof pillars and a sloping rear. Examples vary between two and four doors; keep the doors and rear side windows consistent. Its steel body has crisp edges, modest chrome or black trim, a small VW roundel on the grille and Passat lettering on the rear. Period cars often show faded paint, sun-worn seats and simple steel wheels. It sits well below an SUV’s waistline. The doors shut with a light metallic clack; the petrol engine idles roughly and grows louder as the car pulls away.

For a recognizable classic, depict a 1964 Chevrolet Impala: a broad, low American car with a long bonnet, wide chrome grille, paired round headlights on each side and three round taillights on each side. Its nearly horizontal body lines, bright window trim and small Impala badges belong on a steel body much longer than a modern compact sedan. A four-door sedan has framed side windows and a spacious bench-seat cabin. Chrome bumpers reflect the pavement in hard highlights. The car leans gently through turns; its heavy doors close with a solid thunk, while the petrol V8, where fitted, has a low uneven idle.

A clear 1980s reference is the Mercedes-Benz W123 sedan. It has a long, flat bonnet, upright chrome-framed grille with the three-pointed star above it, large rectangular headlamp assemblies and a squared-off boot. Thick doors, restrained chrome strips and a high glass cabin give it a substantial shape without SUV height. Inside are broad seats, a large thin-rimmed steering wheel and plainly marked analogue gauges. Beige, cream and silver paint are plausible in Iraqi traffic. The suspension lets the body settle softly after a bump. Doors close with a dense thud; a diesel example idles with a distinct rhythmic clatter.

Use a Changan CS75 Plus when a specific contemporary Changan SUV is needed. It is a mid-size, five-door crossover with a tall nose, broad patterned grille, narrow angular LED lamps and dark lower bumper openings. The Changan emblem sits centrally on the grille; model lettering belongs at the rear. Large alloy wheels fill dark-edged arches, and a roof spoiler projects above the rear window. Its cabin places two front seats above a raised centre console, with screens across the dashboard. The body rolls slightly over a speed hump. Doors make a padded clunk; tyres hiss on asphalt and the engine becomes audible during acceleration.

For a specific, everyday Geely, show an Emgrand sedan rather than a generic badge on an invented body. It is a compact four-door car with a short, rounded bonnet, a broad grille carrying the Geely emblem, slim headlamps and a separate boot. The roof arches smoothly over five seats; alloy wheels, body-coloured door handles and narrow rear lamps complete the clean, manufactured look. Geely lettering and Emgrand identification sit on the boot lid, not across the windscreen. In daylight, painted panels show soft reflections. It dips slightly under braking, with ordinary petrol-engine hum, tyre noise and a muted door-closing thump.

For a recognizable Haval, use the H6 crossover. Its tall five-door body has a wide grille with the Haval name at the front, slim headlamps extending toward the wings and black trim around the lower body and wheel arches. A high roof, rear hatch and broad rear lamps distinguish it from a sedan. Inside, the driver sits upright behind a compact steering wheel, with a central screen above the console. The vehicle is roughly shoulder-high beside an adult. Sunlight catches its grille pattern and curved side panels. It rocks lightly over uneven pavement; doors shut with a heavy thump, followed by tyre hum and subdued engine noise.

Use an MG5 sedan to make an unspecified modern MG visually consistent. It is a low, compact four-door car with a sloping roofline, a large dark front grille bearing the silver octagonal MG badge, swept-back headlamps and a short raised boot. The same octagonal badge appears at the rear, with MG5 lettering nearby. Its alloy wheels are modest in size compared with the body, and the cabin has front bucket seats, rear seating and a central dashboard screen. Gloss paint gives clear highlights under streetlights. It moves with little body roll on smooth roads; expect tyre hiss, a restrained petrol-engine note and a light door clunk.

The Tesla Cybertruck is a large electric pickup made of flat, unpainted stainless-steel-looking panels. Its roof rises to a sharp central peak and slopes toward the short rear bed, whose tonneau cover can conceal the cargo space. A continuous narrow light bar spans the blunt front; dark glass, angular wheel arches and a full-width rear light reinforce the geometric shape. There is no conventional front grille or exhaust pipe. It stands taller and considerably wider than a person, with a high cabin floor. Straight panels throw broad, hard reflections. It accelerates without engine revs, producing electric whine, tyre noise and a solid door-closing sound.

A full-size, high-clearance four-wheel-drive SUV, often white with blue police markings, dark windows and an Arabic الشرطة label on the doors or side panels. Model, stripe pattern and badge placement vary by department; do not give every vehicle identical graphics. A red-and-blue light bar sits across the roof, with a siren speaker behind the grille or beneath the bar. Large tyres, side mirrors and a rear tailgate give it the proportions of a working patrol vehicle. It rolls firmly over speed bumps, its body rocking slightly. Engine and tyre noise dominate until the siren sounds. Show officers in uniform beside it on Iraqi streets.

A road-going police motorcycle with a tall windshield, broad front fairing, mirrors on both sides and hard storage cases flanking the rear wheel. Traffic-police bikes vary by model, but white bodywork with blue markings and Arabic police lettering makes the role legible. Small blue or red warning lamps may sit near the fairing or rear cases. The rider sits upright in a helmet and traffic-police uniform, feet on the ground when directing stopped vehicles. At low speed the bike leans gently into turns; its suspension dips under braking. Expect a steady engine note, sharper acceleration and an occasional short siren burst amid street traffic.

A tall, boxy city bus painted strong red, with two horizontal rows of windows and a clearly visible upper passenger deck. Its height is roughly twice that of a nearby car. Arabic route information may appear behind the front glass; fleet markings and grille details depend on the particular bus. Passengers enter through a curbside door and climb an interior stair, while seated riders are visible at both window levels. The long body swings wide around corners and sways more at the top than at street level. In daylight, broad windows reflect shopfronts and trees. The diesel engine rumbles beneath conversation, footsteps and the hiss or clatter of the passenger door.

A compact cab-over pickup: the short, nearly flat front puts the driver above the front axle, and a low open cargo bed extends behind the two-door cab. A Kia badge sits on the front grille; exact grille and headlamp shapes vary by model year. The bed has metal side panels and a hinged tailgate, often carrying stacked crates, sacks or shop supplies secured with rope. Beside an adult, the roof is only modestly taller, but the loaded bed extends well past the cab. The small diesel engine rattles at idle; the leaf-sprung rear bounces over uneven pavement, and loose cargo or side panels clank.

A medium or large truck carries a long cylindrical metal water tank on its chassis, with rounded ends, a top filling hatch and pipes or valves at the rear or side. A hose is coiled on a rack or laid beside the truck during delivery. Paint varies—white, blue and unpainted metal are all plausible—and any drinking-water wording should match the vehicle’s actual service. The tank sits higher than the cab rails and adds visible weight: the truck starts slowly, brakes early and rocks over potholes. Water splashes through the hose into a building tank or container, with pump vibration, a diesel idle and the occasional metallic tap of a valve.

A small or medium delivery truck carries ice in an insulated box body or beneath a heavy cover, depending on the supplier. The cargo area has plain pale panels, a rear loading door and a metal step or bumper; melting water may drip near the threshold. Workers unload rectangular blocks with tongs or move bagged ice in stacks, keeping the doors open only briefly in the heat. The truck sits slightly lower on its suspension when full. Under hard sunlight, wet patches shine on the pavement while the insulated walls remain opaque. Expect diesel idling, a rear latch clanking, plastic bags rustling or solid ice scraping across a loading surface.

A heavy truck has a cab up front and a deep enclosed refuse body behind it, usually ending in a broad rear loading hopper. Fleet colours and municipal markings vary; the important parts are the rear lip, lifting mechanism and hydraulic compactor, not a perfectly clean paint finish. Workers bring wheeled bins or loose bags to the back, step away, then operate the lift or compression cycle. The truck crawls between stops, air brakes sighing. Hydraulic pumps whine as the mechanism rises and presses inward; bin wheels rattle over pavement and metal containers knock against the loading edge. Work lights make the rear opening visible at dawn.

A compact, heavy-looking security vehicle has an enclosed box body or reinforced van shell, small thick-glass windows and sturdy, closely fitted rear or side doors. Visible hinges, reinforced door frames and multiple locks distinguish it from an ordinary delivery van. Its paint and company lettering vary by operator; avoid invented bank logos or exposed stacks of money. The vehicle rides low on strong suspension, turns deliberately and pauses close to a bank entrance. Staff in work uniforms transfer sealed cases through a controlled doorway. The scene sounds like a diesel engine idling, firm door latches clicking and footsteps on pavement, with ordinary traffic continuing around it.

The Boeing 787 is a long, wide-body passenger jet with two large engines beneath swept wings. Its wingtips taper to narrow, upward-curving points rather than carrying upright winglets. The rear edges of the engine nacelles have distinctive serrated chevrons. Airline colours vary, but the smooth fuselage, rounded nose and tall tail retain the same proportions. It stands well above ground crew, with passenger doors reached by a jet bridge or high stairs. During takeoff the wings flex visibly upward; on landing they settle as speed falls. Engine sound rises from a low rushing hum to a powerful, even roar.

topic: Airbus A320 with Iraqi Airways livery
body: This is a narrow-body, twin-engine Airbus A320: one passenger aisle, one engine beneath each wing, a rounded nose and compact wings ending in upright wingtip devices on aircraft so equipped. Iraqi Airways colours give it a mostly white fuselage, green airline titles in Arabic and English near the front, and a green vertical tail bearing the white stylized bird emblem. The passenger doors are small relative to a jet bridge; rows of oval windows run along the cabin. Ground staff and baggage carts reach roughly to the lower fuselage. Taxiing is steady, with turning nose wheels and a continuous engine whine that deepens during takeoff.

A typical large cargo jet resembles an airliner in wings, cockpit and engines but has few or no cabin windows. A broad cargo door sits high on the forward side of the fuselage, opening to admit palletized freight on a lifting loader; a smaller crew door is nearby. Its white or company-coloured body is much taller than the workers beneath it, and its landing gear has multiple heavy wheels. On the apron, loaders rise slowly into position while containers roll into the hold. Taxiing and takeoff are deliberate, with a low engine rumble becoming a sustained roar; hydraulic equipment adds brief mechanical whines.

A common small floatplane has a high wing, one propeller at the nose and two long, narrow metal floats beneath the fuselage. Angled struts connect the floats to the body, holding the cabin above spray; each float has a stepped underside that helps it lift clear of the water. Passengers climb from a dock into a compact cabin, not through an airport jet bridge. At low speed the floats push small bow waves. As the propeller pulls harder, spray trails behind and the aircraft skims on its float steps before lifting off. The sound is a steady propeller buzz over splashing water.

A gyrocopter is a light, usually one- or two-seat aircraft with a large rotor overhead and a separate propeller, commonly mounted behind the seats. It has a narrow frame, small wheels and a tail with vertical fins; some models have an open cockpit, others a clear enclosure. Unlike a helicopter, its rotor turns freely in the airflow during flight while the propeller supplies forward thrust. Before departure, the rotor may be spun up on the ground; the aircraft then rolls along a runway and climbs at a modest forward angle. Rotor blades make a rhythmic swish above the sharper buzz of the engine and propeller.

A hot air balloon has a huge rounded fabric envelope, often made of bright coloured panels, tapering to an open mouth above a small wicker passenger basket. Strong cables join the basket to the burner frame and envelope. On the ground, a fan first fills the fabric; short blasts from the propane burner heat the air until the envelope rises upright. Passengers stand inside the waist-high basket while the balloon drifts with the wind rather than steering like an aircraft. The burner makes a loud rushing flame, followed by quiet intervals with faint fabric rustling. At landing, the basket may bump and tip gently.

A racing yacht has a long, narrow hull, a tall mast and a deep keel below the waterline. Its large triangular mainsail rises behind the mast, while a foresail stretches toward the bow; many have a low cockpit and winches for tightening ropes. Hulls are commonly white or brightly painted, with dark windows and sponsor markings that vary by team. Crew members in life jackets move across the deck to balance the boat as it leans under wind pressure. During a turn, sails briefly flap before filling on the opposite side. Water hisses along the hull, ropes strain through winches and loose sailcloth snaps sharply.

An Iraqi passenger river ferry is a low motorboat built for short crossings on the Tigris or Euphrates. A practical version has a painted metal or wooden hull, open sides with handrails, simple bench seats and a light canopy shading passengers from the strong sun. Its deck sits close to the water, so people step aboard from a landing or short gangplank rather than climbing high stairs. The driver eases away from the bank, turns into the current and approaches the opposite landing slowly. The motor makes a steady rattling hum; small waves slap the hull while passengers talk over the wind and river noise.

A working fishing trawler has a blunt steel or fiberglass hull, a wheelhouse above the main deck, railings, antennas, and powerful winches beside coils of thick rope. A stern trawler leaves its rear deck open for hauling a net over a roller or ramp; wet mesh, floats, and metal doors lie nearby. Paint is often scuffed and stained around the working areas. It moves heavily through waves, pitching more than a large ship, with a foamy wake behind it. A diesel engine drones beneath the clatter of winches, gull calls, and water slapping the hull.

An ocean-going oil tanker is an exceptionally long, broad ship with a dark red or black hull, a low, nearly flat cargo deck, and a white or pale superstructure near the stern. Parallel pipes run along the deck between raised fittings, access hatches, and a manifold area. No open oil is visible: the cargo is inside sealed tanks. From a distance, people on deck look tiny against the ship’s length. The tanker turns slowly and leaves a wide, subdued wake rather than racing spray. At close range, engines hum low, ventilation fans whir, and waves wash against the hull.

A MagSafe wallet sits flat against the center of a compatible iPhone’s back, below its raised camera lenses. The wallet is a slim, rounded rectangle, usually leather or woven synthetic material, about the width of a payment card and shorter than the phone. Its outer face may show a small embossed Apple logo; cards remain mostly hidden, with their edges accessible through the wallet’s opening. Magnets hold it in place, so it moves with the phone but can be peeled off by hand. The metal-and-glass phone gives a faint tap when set down; removing the wallet makes a soft rubbing sound.

A book-style foldable phone looks like a thick, narrow smartphone when closed, with a usable screen on the outside and a visible hinge along one long edge. Opened slowly with both hands, it becomes a small, nearly square tablet. The flexible inner display has a faint vertical crease where it bends; it does not fold as sharply as paper. Rear cameras project from one outer panel, and the two halves sit close together when shut. The hinge resists movement smoothly and ends in a muted click. Finger taps are quiet, while reflections shift across the glossy screens as the phone opens.

An Apple Watch has a small rounded-rectangle case with curved glass, a touchscreen, and a band attached flush at its short ends. Aluminum and stainless-steel models have a clean metallic finish; common bands are soft silicone, woven fabric, or linked metal. On a standard right-handed setup, the Digital Crown and side button sit on the right edge, though the display orientation can be reversed. The watch rests close to the wrist rather than dangling. A raised wrist wakes the screen, a finger swipes through bright icons, and the Crown turns with small tactile ticks. Alerts make restrained chimes or wrist vibrations.

An AirPods charging case is a palm-sized, glossy white plastic shell with smoothly rounded edges and a thin seam around its hinged lid. A tiny status light sits on the front; a charging port is centered on the bottom. Opening the lid exposes two fitted wells holding the earbuds upright by their stems. The lid pivots from the back, stops firmly, and closes with a crisp magnetic snap. The earbuds lift out with slight magnetic resistance. The case has no large exterior branding. Under daylight its surface shows soft reflections and fine scratches; its sounds are small clicks, not electronic beeps.

Apple Vision Pro has a curved, dark glass front set in a smooth aluminum frame, with a soft light seal pressed around the eyes. A woven band wraps around the back of the head, and a separate top strap may support its weight. A cable runs from the headset to a pocket-sized external battery. The Digital Crown and a second button sit on its upper edge. Cameras and sensors face outward; users interact mainly by looking, pinching their fingers, and speaking, without handheld controllers. It is worn over the eyes, not balanced on the nose. Close up, fabric brushes softly and cooling fans are faint.

A typical standalone VR headset is a rigid plastic visor, wider than a face, with dark camera and sensor windows on its front. Foam or fabric padding seals gently around the eyes, while an adjustable strap holds the visor against the face and around the back of the head. Two handheld controllers, when supplied, track each hand separately. The wearer turns their whole head to look around and may reach into empty air, while the physical headset stays fixed against the face. The visor blocks a direct view of the wearer’s eyes. Strap adjustments rustle, controllers click, and built-in speakers play close, directional sound.

A typical smart speaker is a small upright cylinder, about the height of a drinking glass, with tightly woven fabric covering its sides and a hard plastic top and base. Tiny microphone openings and touch controls sit on top; a narrow light ring or small indicator glows when it responds. A power cable exits near the bottom and runs to a wall socket. It stays still on a shelf or table while people speak to it from across the room. Its reply comes from the fabric-covered body, with clear speech and soft bass; a brief chime may mark a request. In daylight, the fabric shows a fine, even texture.

A smart doorbell camera is a slim, palm-length rectangle mounted vertically beside an entrance door, usually in dark plastic with a contrasting faceplate. A small camera lens and sometimes an infrared sensor sit above a large, clearly marked push button. The button’s light ring may glow or flash; it is not a screen. Screws are usually concealed under the faceplate or mounting plate. A visitor presses the button once, producing a short indoor chime and a faint click outdoors. The camera itself does not swivel: its wide-angle view remains fixed on the doorway. Porch lighting reflects in its glossy lens while the surrounding casing stays matte.

A common outdoor security camera has a compact white metal or plastic bullet-shaped housing, roughly the length of an adult hand, fixed to a wall by a circular mounting plate and short adjustable arm. A dark glass circle at the front contains the lens, with small infrared LEDs sometimes arranged around it. A cable disappears through the mounting plate or runs in a protective conduit. Once installed, this fixed camera does not track people; its angle changes only when someone adjusts the bracket. It is normally silent, though nearby wind or rain may be audible. Sunlight casts a sharp shadow beneath its housing, and dust often settles along the upper edge.

A home Wi-Fi router is a low rectangular plastic box, often black or white, sitting flat on a shelf with vents along its sides or underside. Two or more slim antennas may rise from the back on hinged joints. Power and Ethernet cables plug into a row of ports at the rear, beside a small power socket; printed port labels are tiny. Along the front or top edge, separate green, blue, or amber LEDs indicate power, internet, and Wi-Fi activity. Some stay steady while others blink irregularly as data passes. The router itself does not move and is nearly silent, with only occasional faint electronic coil noise in a quiet room.

A power bank is a dense, phone-sized slab with rounded corners, usually matte plastic or anodized metal and noticeably thick for its footprint. USB-A and USB-C sockets sit together along one short edge, often beside a small button. Tiny printed capacity and electrical ratings are usually on the back or bottom; a row of pin-sized LEDs or a small numeric display shows remaining charge when pressed. A person holds it in one hand or leaves it beside a phone while a cable links the two. It makes no operating sound. Under a lamp, its edges catch a soft highlight, while scuffs and fingerprints show where it is regularly handled.

A phone charging cable is a flexible insulated cord, commonly around one metre long, with a molded connector housing at each end. One end may be USB-A or USB-C for a charger; the phone end is a smaller USB-C, Lightning, or Micro-USB plug, depending on the device. The metal tips are rigid, while strain-relief sleeves let the cord bend gradually behind them. When connected, the cable hangs in a loose curve rather than a perfectly straight line and may twist on a tabletop. Insertion makes a small plastic-and-metal click; charging itself is silent. White cables pick up grey marks near frequently gripped ends.

A selfie stick has a narrow handgrip, nested telescoping metal tubes, and a spring-loaded phone clamp at the far end. Folded, it is about the length of a hand; extended, the slim sections step down in diameter toward the phone. Rubber pads inside the clamp protect the screen edges, and a small hinge lets the phone tilt toward the holder. A thumb button on the grip or a separate Bluetooth remote triggers the camera. The tubes slide out with a light scrape and stop firmly; the extended stick can sway slightly with a walking arm. It is held away from the face, with the phone angled back toward one or several people.

A phone gimbal is a handheld motorized stabilizer with a thick grip, control buttons, and three small rotating motor housings linked by short arms. A padded clamp holds the phone horizontally or vertically above the grip, offset so the arms can rotate without striking it. The phone must be seated securely; when powered on, the motors level it with a quiet hum and tiny corrective movements. As a person walks and turns their wrist, the handle bobs but the camera points smoothly along its chosen direction. A thumb joystick changes its angle, while a trigger may lock or recenter it. Matte plastic and metal edges catch moving highlights outdoors.

A palm-sized rectangular camera with rounded corners, a wide-angle lens projecting slightly from the front, and a small front status screen or indicator beside it. The rear is mostly a colour touchscreen. Its plastic or metal body has a textured finish, tiny microphone openings, a top shutter button, and a sealed side door for the battery, memory card and charging port. Branding, when visible, sits on the front and varies by model. It clips into a frame or mount, often on a helmet, handlebar or handheld grip. Movement produces wide-angle edge distortion; operation brings brief button clicks and soft electronic beeps.

A cinema camera rig is an assembled system rather than one fixed camera shape. A boxy camera body sits behind a large interchangeable lens, often with a rectangular matte box at the front. Two parallel metal rods may run beneath the lens, supporting the matte box and a follow-focus wheel at one side. A top handle, side grip, outward-facing monitor, cables and rear battery make the silhouette uneven and substantial. Brand marks belong to individual components, not the whole rig. An operator supports it by hand or mounts it on a tripod. Focus adjustments turn smoothly with faint gear sounds; handling adds small clicks and cable rustle.

A typical vocal studio microphone is a large-diaphragm condenser: a metal cylinder roughly hand-length, with a rounded mesh grille covering its upper section. It hangs upright in a circular elastic shock mount on a boom stand, with a thin XLR cable plugged into the bottom. A round fabric pop filter sits a few inches in front of the grille, between the singer and microphone. Small switches or branding, if present, are on the body and vary by model. The microphone stays still while a performer faces its front side. It makes no sound itself; the stand can creak softly if touched, and the cable connector clicks into place.

Over-ear headphones have two padded oval earcups joined by a curved headband, with sliding arms to adjust their height. Soft synthetic leather or fabric cushions surround the ears; the outer cups are usually plastic or metal, sometimes bearing a manufacturer mark. Left and right labels appear near the hinges or inside the band. A wired pair has a cable leaving one or both cups, while a wireless pair has small buttons and a charging port. The cups swivel slightly as someone puts them on and settle against the head. Adjustment produces light plastic clicks; rubbing a cable or cushion makes faint handling noise.

A gaming chair typically has a tall, thickly padded back with a headrest and raised side bolsters, plus a separate cushioned seat. Upholstery is often black synthetic leather or woven fabric with coloured panels and visible stitching. Adjustable armrests flank the seat; beneath it are a tilt mechanism, gas-lift cylinder and five-spoke base with small swivel casters. Some models have removable neck and lower-back pillows attached by straps. Logos, when present, usually appear near the headrest. A seated person can swivel, roll and lean back; the casters rattle lightly on hard floors, while tilt and height controls click or hiss briefly.

An RGB gaming keyboard is a low rectangular board with raised rows of keys and light visible through their translucent legends and the gaps around them. The frame is usually dark plastic or metal; some models add a detachable wrist rest, media controls or a volume wheel along the upper edge. Key labels sit on the keycaps, while any manufacturer logo is usually on the frame. A cable commonly exits from the rear, though wireless models exist. RGB lighting can hold one colour or shift in waves across individual keys. Fingers press the keys a few millimetres; the sound ranges from soft taps to distinct mechanical clacks, depending on the switches.

A mechanical keyboard has a rigid rectangular case containing individual switches beneath separate, removable keycaps. The keys sit in staggered rows with longer keys for space, shift and enter; legends are printed or moulded on their tops. Case materials range from plastic to aluminium, and the cable socket is generally at the rear. Lighting is optional: many mechanical keyboards have none. Each key travels downward against a spring and returns when released, producing a series of crisp taps, clicks or muted thocks depending on its switch and construction. A typist’s fingers move across the rows while the keyboard itself stays flat on a desk.

A non-display graphic drawing tablet is a thin, flat rectangular panel resting on a desk, with a slightly textured active area marked by subtle corner indicators. One side may carry a column of programmable buttons and a small manufacturer mark; a cable or wireless connection links it to a computer. Its matching stylus is pen-shaped, with a pointed replaceable nib and often two side buttons. An artist watches the computer screen while moving the pen across the tablet. The cursor follows the nib’s position, and pressure changes the digital line width. The hand glides lightly; nib contact makes a faint scratch or tap.

A desktop filament 3D printer is a roughly 40-centimetre-wide machine with a rigid metal frame, a flat square print bed and a small print head riding on horizontal rails. A plastic filament spool sits on a holder above or beside the frame, feeding a thin strand into the heated nozzle. Belts move the head in short, precise lines while the bed or gantry shifts between layers. A partly finished object shows fine horizontal ridges. The screen and controls are usually on the front; markings depend on the manufacturer. In a workshop or home, it makes soft fan noise, motor whirring and brief mechanical clicks.

A robot vacuum is a low, round plastic disc, usually about 30–35 centimetres across and short enough to pass under many sofas. Its top has a start button and, on some models, a raised circular navigation sensor. A bumper wraps around the front edge; underneath are wheels, a spinning side brush and a central suction opening. It rolls steadily over tile or rugs, turns when it approaches furniture and occasionally pauses to reorient itself. A compact charging dock rests against a wall with contacts near floor level. In a lived-in home it produces a continuous fan hum, faint brush rattle and small taps against chair legs.

A household air purifier is an upright plastic appliance, commonly white or dark grey, standing about knee to waist height. Perforations or narrow grilles on its sides or front admit room air; a larger grille on top releases a gentle upward flow. Behind a removable panel sits a thick, pleated filter, invisible when the unit is closed. A small display or touch buttons near the top show fan settings, sometimes with a coloured air-quality indicator. It stays stationary on a clear patch of floor, away from curtains. Its sound is a low, even fan rush that grows louder at higher settings, without visible vapour.

A common portable electric radiant heater is a rectangular appliance, about knee height, on two short feet. A metal grille covers horizontal quartz tubes or heating elements; when switched on, the elements glow orange behind the grille. A painted metal or heat-resistant plastic casing surrounds them, with switches or a dial on one side and an electrical cord exiting near the base. It stands still on a level floor, facing people seated nearby, with clear space in front. Its light casts a warm orange tint on nearby surfaces. It may click as its thermostat switches and give off a faint electrical hum, but has no flame or smoke.

An Iraqi kerosene sobba is a freestanding metal heater with a fuel reservoir at its base and a vertical burner section above it. Common versions have a round or boxy painted-steel body, a protective perforated metal guard and a control knob that raises or lowers the wick. Some connect to a stovepipe; the pipe should appear only on a model built for one. When lit, a small, steady flame heats the metal, which gradually darkens and radiates warmth. It remains stationary while people sit nearby in a winter room. Refilling happens only when it is off and cool. Expect a soft burner hiss and occasional metal ticks as it warms.

A traditional tabletop oil lamp has a rounded glass or metal reservoir below a narrow metal burner. A flat cotton wick passes through the burner, and a small side wheel adjusts how much wick is exposed. A tall, clear glass chimney surrounds the flame, open at the top to let hot air rise. The lamp is small enough to carry in one hand but stands upright on a broad, stable base. When lit, its yellow flame flickers gently and throws soft shadows across a table or wall; it gives no sharp beam. The burner may click as the wheel turns, while the flame is nearly silent.

A Ramadan fanous is a decorative lantern with a small base, a wider middle, a tapered or domed metal top and a loop for carrying or hanging. Many have thin brass-coloured or painted metal frames around coloured glass or translucent plastic panels. Cutout stars, crescents or geometric patterns may decorate the upper metalwork. Sizes range from hand-held pieces to larger lanterns displayed beside a doorway. An electric light inside makes the panels glow red, blue, green or amber and casts patterned patches nearby. When carried, the lantern swings slightly from its handle; metal versions make a light clink. It appears in homes and shop displays during Ramadan.

A chandelier hangs from a ceiling mount by a short chain or central stem, with its weight supported overhead. A common home design has a polished brass-coloured or chrome centre and several curved arms arranged evenly around it. Each arm ends in an upward-facing lamp holder, often covered by a small fabric shade or glass cup; decorative glass drops may hang below. Its total width is often comparable to a dining table’s narrower dimension, leaving headroom underneath. When switched on, the bulbs cast overlapping warm pools of light and glints on glass or metal. It remains almost motionless, though hanging drops can make a faint chime if disturbed.

A narrow, flexible white or copper-coloured circuit tape carries evenly spaced, square LED packages and tiny resistors. Printed cut marks divide it into short sections; adhesive backing sticks it beneath shelves, inside ceiling coves or along cabinet edges. A low-voltage cable connects one end to a power supply, which is usually hidden. The tape bends around gentle curves but does not hang in sharp folds. Individual light points may show on a bare strip; behind a frosted diffuser they merge into a continuous line. White versions give steady light, while RGB versions change colour together or in segments. The strip itself is silent.

A traditional neon sign is made from slender glass tubes bent into letters or outlines, held slightly away from a backing by small clear supports. Dark electrode housings and insulated wires appear at the tube ends, leading to a transformer mounted out of sight or behind the sign. Lit tubes form continuous, intensely coloured strokes rather than separate dots; red-orange neon can glow through clear glass, while other colours use different gas mixtures or coated glass. The glow casts soft colour onto a nearby wall or shop window. It switches on at once, sometimes with a faint electrical hum, and otherwise has no moving parts.

A countertop espresso grinder has a clear bean hopper above a solid metal or plastic body, with a numbered adjustment collar near the burr chamber. Ground coffee exits a short chute into a portafilter held on a fork below; some models dispense into a separate cup. A button or switch starts the motor, and beans drop from the hopper as they are crushed between hidden burrs. The sound is a steady, sharp mechanical whirr with a dry rattling undertone, stopping abruptly when the motor cuts out. Fine brown grounds collect in a small mound and may scatter lightly around the chute. A power cord trails behind it.

A French press is a straight-sided glass or stainless-steel cylinder with a pouring spout, a handle and a fitted lid. A thin rod passes through the lid to a round knob; below it, a metal mesh screen nearly fills the cylinder. Coarse coffee grounds float and swirl when hot water is poured in, then settle during steeping. The user presses the knob down slowly, pushing the mesh through the liquid while the grounds remain beneath it. Glass models show a dark coffee layer above the screen. The plunger moves with gentle resistance and a faint scrape; pouring makes a soft liquid trickle, not a pressurised hiss.

A classic moka pot is a small, often octagonal aluminium vessel in three screwed-together sections. The lower water chamber has a small safety valve on its side; a funnel-shaped basket sits inside it, and a perforated filter lies beneath the upper collector. The top has a short pouring spout, a hinged lid with a knob and a dark heat-resistant handle set away from the metal. On a stove, steam pressure drives coffee upward through the central opening into the top chamber. A thin stream appears first, followed by bubbling foam and a hollow sputtering sound. The metal grows hot; the handle remains the place to grip it.

A Turkish coffee sand heater is a countertop metal box or round tray filled almost to the rim with fine, pale sand heated from underneath. Its outer rim stays visible, often in dark painted metal or stainless steel, with a switch or temperature control on the base. A small long-handled cezve sits partly buried in the sand, upright, while its handle extends safely over the edge. The seller shifts the pot through the hot grains for even heating, leaving shallow furrows. Dark coffee rises into a thick tan foam near the lip, then the pot is lifted before it spills. Sand rustles softly; the coffee gives a faint simmer.

An Iraqi-style charcoal samovar is a tall polished metal hot-water urn with a broad base, a central chimney for coals and a small tap projecting low from its side. Its shoulders narrow toward a top opening where a small teapot can rest and stay warm. The reflective body may be stainless steel or plated metal, with sturdy side handles for carrying it when cool. Burning charcoal heats the water around the chimney; a faint red glow may be visible through lower air vents. Water flows from the tap in a narrow stream into a tea glass. Coals crackle quietly, and boiling water produces a low, sustained murmur.

An Iraqi tea kettle stack has a larger metal kettle below and a smaller teapot, the qouri, seated securely above its lid opening. The lower kettle is usually stainless steel or aluminium, with a curved spout and a side handle; the upper pot may be glazed ceramic or metal, with its own lid, spout and handle. Steam from the lower kettle keeps concentrated black tea warm upstairs. To serve, a person pours a little dark tea from the qouri into a small clear glass, then adds hot water from the kettle to adjust its strength. Lids tap lightly, water splashes, and the kettle may hiss softly on the stove.

A tea glass holder is a small metal cradle sized for one narrow-waisted istikan glass, not a full-sized mug. A circular base supports the glass, while an openwork sleeve or several curved metal strips rise around its lower half; a small handle projects from one side. Common finishes are silver-coloured steel or brass-coloured metal, sometimes stamped with a simple floral pattern. The clear glass remains visible above the rim of the holder, showing amber tea. A person lifts it by the handle, leaving the hot glass untouched. Set on a tabletop, it makes a light metallic tap; the glass gives a higher clink against the frame.

A table sugar bowl is a palm-sized vessel placed beside tea glasses and a teapot. It may be white ceramic, clear glass or polished metal, usually with a round body, a flat base and a removable lid with a small central knob. Some lids have a notch at the rim for a teaspoon; others close fully, with the spoon resting alongside. White granulated sugar forms a level or slightly mounded surface inside. Fingers lift the lid by its knob, and a spoon scoops or stirs a portion into tea. Ceramic lids click softly against their rims, while a metal spoon rings against glass or steel.

A large Iraqi cooking pot, or jidir, is a deep, wide metal vessel with straight or gently flared sides, a flat base and two short handles fixed opposite each other near the rim. Plain aluminium is common, with a dull silver surface darkened or scratched from repeated use; stainless-steel versions are brighter. A broad, slightly domed lid sits on top by its central knob. Beside an adult at the stove, the pot can reach from knee to mid-thigh height. It holds rice, broth or stew and must be lifted with both hands when full. Steam escapes at the lid edge, with a low simmer inside and an occasional lid rattle.

A rice serving tray is a broad, shallow round platter, often stainless steel or aluminium, with a low raised rim that keeps grains from spilling. Its diameter can span much of a dining table, requiring two hands to carry when loaded. Cooked white rice sits in a loose mound rather than a firm mould; individual long grains catch the light, with meat, nuts or vegetables sometimes arranged on top. The metal underneath is usually visible around the edge. A server sets the tray down level, producing a brief metal-on-table sound, then portions rice with a broad spoon. Spoon strokes make soft scraping sounds beneath the rustle of loose grains.

A dolma pot is typically a wide, deep cooking pot with a heavy, flat base and two side handles, sized to hold tightly packed layers of stuffed vegetables and leaves. It may be dull aluminium or stainless steel; there is no special exterior logo or distinctive moulded shape. Open it to show glossy grape-leaf rolls, peppers or onions fitted closely together, often beneath an inverted heatproof plate that keeps them submerged and in place. A lid covers the pot as it cooks over a low flame. Liquid bubbles quietly at the edges, steam beads under the lid, and the plate may make a faint ceramic knock when the contents shift.

A clay tannour is an upright, thick-walled oven with a circular opening at the top and an interior that narrows toward the bottom. Its exterior is rough earth-brown clay or plaster, sometimes set into a masonry surround; the inner wall is darker and heat-stained. Glowing fuel and ash sit below the baking area, while orange light flickers up the curved walls. A baker leans over the opening and presses a flattened round of dough against the hot inner wall using a padded tool. The bread stays vertical as it blisters, then is lifted free with a metal hook. Fire crackles underneath, with a faint hiss as fresh dough meets clay.

A charcoal mangal is a long, shallow rectangular metal firebox, commonly dark steel, with an open top and short legs that lift it above the ground. Charcoal fills the trough in a low, even bed; narrow upper edges support kebab skewers laid crosswise, with their handles projecting beyond one side. Small air holes may run along the lower sidewalls. In a courtyard, roadside stall or outdoor eating area, a cook turns the skewers by hand to expose each face to the heat. The charcoal glows red beneath grey ash, fat drips and sizzles, and brief wisps of smoke rise through the food without hiding its shape.

Iraqi kebab skewers are long, flat metal strips rather than thin round wires. Their broad, straight blades hold pressed minced meat along the centre so it resists spinning; a narrower bare section forms a handgrip at one end, sometimes finished with a twist or loop. The metal is silver-grey steel, darkened in places by heat. Several skewers lie parallel across a charcoal grill, each extending well beyond its edges so the handles remain reachable. A cook rotates each skewer in measured turns, keeping the meat facing the coals. The steel lightly clicks against the grill rim, while the meat sizzles and releases small drops of fat.

A household stovetop pressure cooker is a deep, thick-walled aluminum or stainless-steel pot, roughly 22–26 cm across, with a flat base and a heavy lid that locks against a rubber sealing ring. A long handle or two short side handles keep hands away from the hot body. The lid has a small pressure valve on top and often a separate safety vent; neither is a spout. It sits on a gas burner or electric hob, not inside an oven. Steam may escape in brief white wisps, accompanied by a steady hiss or occasional valve rattle. Polished metal catches sharp kitchen reflections, while the handles remain matte black or dark grey.

A countertop food processor has a low, heavy motor base and a clear plastic bowl locked onto it, usually with a central spindle rising through the bowl.
